parts: Lesson 7: Performing Art Heritage in India — Summary

Indian music has three broad forms: Hindustani (a blend of Indo-Turko-Persian styles), Carnatic (South Indian, linked to bhakti saints and temple rituals from the 8th century and the guru-shishya tradition) and folk music (of the common people and regions; Dom, Mirasi, Manganiar and Langa communities; in Kashmir Chhakri, Tambur Naghma and Bcha Naghma). Martial music was played in battles (Hapa Charan and Mian Lal Khan in Akbar's time; the Dadis of western Rajasthan; the sazindas of Kashmir).

Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), nicknamed Tuti-e-Hind (parrot of India), was born at Patiali, Etah (Uttar Pradesh), and was a disciple of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya. He wrote that Indian music is 'the fire that burns heart and soul' and superior to any other country's. He blended Arabic, Persian and Indian music, is credited with Qawwali and Tarana and with inventing the sitar, and claimed all the ragas of Nayak Gopal as his own. Tansen (born in a Brahmin family of Gwalior) was a disciple of Haridas, served Raja Ram Chand of Baghelkhand and then Akbar, and is considered the composer of the Dhrupad form. Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri records that Sufi Shaikh Salim Chishti wished to hear Tansen sing at his death. The Gwalior (Seniya) Gharana and the Tansen Sangeet Sammelan in Gwalior attract tourists.

Flute (bansuri): a wind instrument in the Vedic texts, associated with Lord Krishna. Tanpura: long-necked string instrument that gives the basic note (4–5 wires). Tabla: percussion; Ustad Zakir Hussain won a Grammy in 1992. Veena: one of the oldest instruments; the Saraswati Veena of South India accompanies Carnatic music. Sitar: plucked, seven strings (five steel, two brass); Pt. Ravi Shankar won the Bharat Ratna in 1999 and three Grammys. Shehnai: aerophonic, played at North Indian weddings and processions; Ustad Bismillah Khan received the Bharat Ratna in 2001. Nagaswaram (Nadaswaram): very long, auspicious instrument of Tamil Nadu temples. Sarod: stringed, from the rebab; Ustad Amjad Ali Khan. Sarangi: bowed, from 'sau rang' (hundred colours), closest to the human voice. Santoor: trapezoid folk instrument of Kashmir played with mezrab (hammers), used in Sufiana kalam. Mridangam: literally 'body of clay', rhythm in Carnatic music (Khol in Bengal). Others: Gottuvadyam, Chenda (Kerala, for Kathakali and Koodiyattam), Rabab (the national instrument of the Arabs; Tansen's disciples were Rababiyas and Beenkaras), Dhol, Dholak, Dhak, Khanjira and Pakhawaj (used in Dhrupad).

Dance in India goes back to the Indus Valley (the torso of a male dancer from Harappa and the dancing girl of Mohenjodaro). It has classical forms (Bharatanatyam, Mohiniattam, Manipuri, Odissi, Kathakali, Kathak, Kuchipudi) and folk forms. Folk dances: Lai Haraoba (Manipur, 'festival of gods'), Karagam (Tamil Nadu, pitchers on heads), Jhika Dasain (Santhal, Jharkhand), Jagar (Kumaun and Garhwal), Bhaktaa (Mayurbhanj, Odisha), Garba (Gujarat, Navratri, 9 nights, around a lamp) and Dandiya (with sticks), Kavadi Aattam (Tamil Nadu, males, balancing a pole with pots), Gidda (Punjab, women only), Ghoomar (Rajasthan, developed by the Bhil tribe, worships goddess Saraswati), Lavani (Maharashtra, Tamasha, dholaki, nine-yard sari), Bihu (Assam), Morulem (Goa, Shigmo festival, peacock feathers), Bhangra (Punjab, harvest, dhol and chimta) and Kalbelia (Rajasthan, snake charmers' tribe).

Drama has dialogue, music and dance (Sanskrit nata, nataka, natya; from nrit, 'to dance'). Its oldest treatise is Bharata's Natyashastra (the fifth Veda). The stage is technically Jarjara, linked to the flag staff of Indra that kept demons away from the performance. Forms: stage performance, street theatre (street corners, socio-political; Tavernier's account of jugglers on the Agra–Surat road), puppet shows and Nukkad Natak (street play on social issues; Safdar Hashmi, Jan Natya Manch).

Puppetry (from Latin pupa, 'doll'; Silappadikaram, 2nd century BC; themes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata): string puppets (Rajasthan, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka), shadow puppets (flat leather figures behind a lit screen; Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka), glove puppets (hand puppets controlled by fingers) and rod puppets (bigger, from below; West Bengal and Odisha).
